name: Lamet

new_statements.quote: A word has the structure (Mi)(Ma)Ma, where Ma is a major syllable, and Mi a minor syllable. [...] The vast majority of the words are of the type Ma, e.g. /ʔɔɔʔ/ 'I', or MiMa, e.g. /rənaah/ 'field'. There are a few examples of MaMa words in the vocabulary, e.g. /ʔarpoor/ (A), /ʔahpooh/ (B) 'evening', and only one MiMaMa word, namely /rəlottot/ 'small owl' in dialect B. The stress falls on the second syllable of two-syllable words. The major syllables in the word /rəlottot/ have the form of a reduplication, and both are stressed. [...] Minor syllables are short and unstressed. (p. 9) — It seems reasonable to assume that both dialects should have tones, or at least contrastive registers, as do other Mon-Khmer languages in the area. However, the material does not allow any investigation of this problem. In the Rəmeet dialect described by Mitani there are two tones. (p. 10)

new_statements.relation_note: Catalog rule '01' (unstressed-stressed, final) is exactly what this states for the dominant MiMa type; the work adds the explicit MaMa/MiMaMa cases and the open question of tone/register. Describes two Laos dialects, A (village Ŋkris) and B (village Talaaŋ), recorded at Lampang in 1974; the PDF on Persée is captcha-gated (not reachable by automated download) but the per-page content endpoint serves the full text of pp. 5-10 (pp. 11-22 are vocabulary tables, image only).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Words are (minor)(major)major; stress falls on the second syllable of two-syllable words, i.e. the final major syllable; minor syllables are short and unstressed. In the single reduplicated MiMaMa word both major syllables are stressed. Tone/register left open: the authors suspect tones or registers exist but their material cannot show it; they cite Mitani's two tones for another dialect.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed; the one three-syllable word /rəlottot/ has both major syllables stressed (reduplication).
new_statements.exceptions: None beyond the reduplicated /rəlottot/ 'small owl' (dialect B) with two stressed major syllables.
new_statements.identity_note: Lindell, Svantesson & Tayanin 1978 describe two Laos dialects, A (village Ŋkris, east of the Nam Tha) and B (Talaaŋ, west of it), and state that Lamet and 'Khamet' are one language of the Palaungic branch. Mitani 1965/1976 describes the Khamet of Wiang Pa Pao, Chiang Rai (Thailand), which Lindell et al. say resembles their dialect B. Charoenma 1980 covers a Lampang informant from Takluh village north of Nam Tha (Ferlus' Lamet A) and the Wiang Pa Pao variety locally called Lua (Ferlus' Khamet). The open copy for the Mitani entry is the 1965 Japanese original (Tōnan Ajia Kenkyū 3(3):22-51), not the 1976 English chapter, which was not found online.

new_statements.quote: 自立音節は terminal juncture の直前に立ちうる音節であって強勢をとることができその実際のメンバーも多い。附属音節は juncture の直前には立たずまた強勢をとることもない。(p. 27) — 自立音節のTの位置に立つ音素すなわちトネームは，カメート語においては(1)高型/ ́/，(2)低型/ ̀/の2つがある。(p. 28) — この問題を考えるためには強勢（stress）や連接（juncture）の記述が先行すべきであるが，これらの音素についてはまだ検討の余地があるので余り深く立ち入らないことにする。2つの音節 S₁ と S₂ とが結合する場合，(1) S₁, S₂ とも強勢をもつ，(2) S₁ が半強勢を，S₂ が強勢をもつ，(3) S₁ は強勢・半強勢をもたず S₂ は強勢をもつ，という3つの場合がある。(pp. 32-33)
new_statements.translation: Major syllables are syllables that can stand immediately before terminal juncture and can take stress, and their actual members are numerous. Minor syllables do not stand immediately before juncture and do not take stress either. (p. 27) — The phonemes that stand in the T position of the major syllable, i.e. the tonemes, are two in Khamet: (1) high /́/ and (2) low /̀/. (p. 28) — To consider this problem [syllable combination] a description of stress and juncture ought to come first, but since there is still room for examination of these phonemes I will not go into them deeply. When two syllables S1 and S2 combine there are three cases: (1) both S1 and S2 carry stress, (2) S1 carries half-stress and S2 stress, (3) S1 carries neither stress nor half-stress and S2 carries stress. (pp. 32-33)
new_statements.citation: Mitani, Yasuyuki. 1976. Descriptive and comparative studies of the Khamet phonology. In Southeast Asia: Nature, Society and Development, 76-95. Kyoto: CSEAS (English ser. 9) / Honolulu: University Press of Hawaii.

new_statements.relation_note: The open copy reached via the listed the Harvard library catalogue/Crossref record is the 1965 Japanese original (Tōnan Ajia Kenkyū 3(3):22-51, DOI 10.20495/tak.3.3_22), of which the listed 1976 English chapter is the translation; the English version itself is not in the Kyoto repository. Placement (final major syllable stressed, minor syllables unstressed) agrees with the catalog's '01'; it adds two lexical tonemes, half-stress, and the caveat that stress/juncture are provisional. Dialect: Khamet of Wiang Pa Pao (Chiang Rai, Thailand), fieldwork 1964-65.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Khamet has two tonemes (high vs. low, the low one with breathy voice) on major syllables; minor syllables mostly take the low toneme. Stress is carried only by major syllables; in any two-syllable combination the second syllable is stressed while the first is stressed, half-stressed, or unstressed (minor syllables only in the last case). So word stress falls on the final (major) syllable, with the author explicitly leaving stress and juncture provisional.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Half-stress (半強勢) on a first major syllable in type (2) combinations, e.g. /jook-luut/; the three degrees are said to shade into one another and alternate freely.
new_statements.exceptions: Type (1) combinations where both syllables are stressed (two full major syllables, /S1 S2/), e.g. /jook luut/ 'deaf'; 'weakened major syllables' (弱まり型自立音節) that stand only in S1 position and shorten their vowel.

Mitani 1965/1976 describes the Khamet of Wiang Pa Pao, Chiang Rai (Thailand), which Lindell et al. say resembles their dialect B. Charoenma 1980 covers a Lampang informant from Takluh village north of Nam Tha (Ferlus' Lamet A) and the Wiang Pa Pao variety locally called Lua (Ferlus' Khamet). new_statements.quote: 2.3.2 The stress group may have one or two syllables. Each stress group has as its nucleus one stressed syllable, which is always the last syllable in the group, and as its periphery it may have an unstressed syllable or a weakly stressed syllable. (p. 27) — 2.5.4.5 Stress. A syllable is said to be stressed if it sticks out or is more prominant than surrounding syllables. Stress in this language is treated as predictable (see sec 2.3). Stress will occur on every monosyllable word. In words with open-transition, or in two syllable words, stress will occur on the last syllable. [...] In conclusion, stress, clarity and pitch are not distinctive in this language. They are predictable and can not distinguish the meaning of a word. Length and register are phonemic features, because they can give new meaning to a word. (p. 76)

new_statements.rule_in_words: Lampang Lamet: the phonological word (stress group) is one or two syllables; its nucleus is one stressed syllable, always the last; a preceding minor syllable is weakly stressed (closed CVC 'minor syllable') or unstressed (open pre-syllable / syllabic nasal). Stress is predictable and non-distinctive; register (and length) are phonemic, pitch is not. For the second language in the thesis, Wiang Pa Pao Lua (= Ferlus' Khamet), the same rule holds (p. 82, p. 126: 'stress will occur on the last syllable'), but that variety 'has two contrastive tones' (p. 80), a falling tone developing from breathy register.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Weakly stressed closed minor syllables (e.g. [pɯt'pumŋ] 'long drum', [pəl'kuul] 'finger') vs. unstressed open pre-syllables; no secondary stress beyond this two-syllable domain.
new_statements.exceptions: None; stress stated as fully predictable. The only intra-thesis difference is between the two varieties: Lampang Lamet has register but no tone, Wiang Pa Pao Lua has two contrastive tones.
new_statements.identity_note: Lindell, Svantesson & Tayanin 1978 describe two Laos dialects, A (village Ŋkris, east of the Nam Tha) and B (Talaaŋ, west of it), and state that Lamet and 'Khamet' are one language of the Palaungic branch. Mitani 1965/1976 describes the Khamet of Wiang Pa Pao, Chiang Rai (Thailand), which Lindell et al. say resembles their dialect B. Charoenma 1980 covers a Lampang informant from Takluh village north of Nam Tha (Ferlus' Lamet A) and the Wiang Pa Pao variety locally called Lua (Ferlus' Khamet). The open copy for the Mitani entry is the 1965 Japanese original (Tōnan Ajia Kenkyū 3(3):22-51), not the 1976 English chapter, which was not found online.

readall_conflicts: On placement there is no disagreement: all three works put stress on the last (major) syllable of the sesquisyllabic word with minor syllables unstressed or weakly stressed. The sources differ on tone: Mitani (Wiang Pa Pao Khamet, 1965) sets up two tonemes (high vs. low/breathy); Charoenma (1980) likewise gives Wiang Pa Pao Lua two contrastive tones but describes Lampang Lamet (Nam Tha origin) as having phonemic register and no distinctive pitch; Lindell et al. (1978, Laos dialects A and B) leave tone/register open, saying their material cannot decide it. Mitani additionally flags his stress and juncture analysis as provisional and allows both syllables of a two-major-syllable compound to be stressed, which Lindell et al. also note for the one reduplicated MiMaMa word.

audit.action: a better source should be cited for the same classification
audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: The classification (fixed-dominant, rule 01 = stress on the final/main syllable of sesquisyllabic words, not strict) rests on Conver 1999, an SIL phonology sketch in MKS 29; the deciding quotation is verbatim on p.37 of the sealang scan downloaded when we checked the sources (no file was held before). Two independent descriptions of a different (Lampang, Lower Lamet) variety, Narumol 1980 MA thesis p.27 and its published condensation Narumol 1982 MKS 11 p.37, both downloaded now, state that the stressed syllable is always the last syllable of the (max. two-syllable) stress group, so three sources across two dialect groups agree. Glottolog lists no reference grammar and web search plus the MKS 44 Palaungic bibliography show no later or instrumental study of Lamet prosody, so Conver 1999 + Narumol 1980/1982 is the best available evidence. sources.quote: 'In a sesquisyllabic word, stress will always fall on the main syllable. That this is a strong characteristic in Lamet is evidenced by the adjustment of loan words to this pattern, given sufficient time. Stress may also be useful as a diagnostic tool to distinguish sesquisyllabic words from compound constructions (i.e., words), which would have stress on both syllables.' p.39: 'because the presyllable is always unstressed, many vowels in this position sound like [schwa-like] in normal paced speech.'
